parties:
Wahida Rashid (Most) and another ----- Petitioners
Vs.
Miron Muhammad Zahidul Hoque ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
2. The opposite party No. 1 as plaintiff filed title suit No. 242 of 1977 in the First Court of Munsif, Kushtia with a prayer for ejectment of the defendant petitioners alleging, inter alia, that the plaintiffs father purchased the suit land in the name of the plaintiff. Thereafter they created building thereon and let out the suit premises at a rental of Tk. 75/- per month to the defendants who undertook to deposit Tk. 7,500/- as security money. They deposited Tk. 6,000/- out of Tk. 7,500/- as security and wanted to deposit rest Tk. 1500/- within one month and taking opportunity of the plaintiffs father's absence, the defendant took key from the minor plaintiff and took possession giving Tk. 450/- as six months advance rent. The defendants are irregular in payment of rent and they became defaulters. The suit premises is required for plaintiffs own business and the plaintiff served notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act upon the defendants asking them to relinquish possession of the suit premises but they did not do so. The defendants being tresspassers in the suit premises are liable to be evicted. 

 3. The defendant petitioners contested the suit by filing a written statement contending, inter alia, that the plaintiffs father took Tk. 7500/- as advance rent from the defendants for construction of the suit premises which was let out to the defendants for running medicine business and for medical practice of the husband of defendant No. 2. The father of the plaintiff took Tk. 6000/- from the husband of defendant No. 1 on 4.12.73. Again one month after Abdur Rashid, husband of the defendant No. 1 paid Tk. 1500/- to the plaintiffs father. The money was paid on condition that the plaintiff would return the said sum of Tk. 7,500/- within 3 years and also adjust the same towards rent in case of any default in payment of rent thereof. The plaintiff did not receive rent for which the defendants were compelled to send rent by money order. No notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act has been served upon the defendants and they are not defaulters and tresspassers. The tenancy commenced from the month of Kartic, 1380 BS and the suit was filed on 24.4.77. The issues as to whether the suit is maintainable in its present form or whether the suit is barred by limitation and whether the plaintiff has any bonafide requirement for the suit premises have been decided in favour of the plaintiff and against the defendants. So the main controversy before the Trial Court was whether the defendants were habitual defaulter and whether the tenancy was determined by the service of notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act and accordingly they are liable to be evicted from the suit premises. Both the courts below have found that the defendants were habitual defaulter and the notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act was duly served upon the defendants and hence the defendants are liable to be evicted from the suit premises. The Trial Court decreed the suit on contest and the court of appeal below on consideration of the evidence on record dismissed the appeal preferred by the defendants and the judgment and decree of the Trial Court was thus upheld. 

 19. Mr. MA Rahim, the learned Advocate for the petitioners, next submits that the learned Courts below committed an error of law in their decision in decreeing the suit with the finding that the defendants are habitual defaulters without considering the fact that an amount of Tk. 6000/- admittedly taken by the plaintiff from the defendants has remained outstanding towards adjustment of the rent and if the said money was allowed to be adjusted, the question of defendants' becoming a defaulter could not have arisen. To counter the aforesaid argument of the learned Advocate for the defendants petitioner Mr. Nizamuddin Haider, appearing for the plaintiff-opposite party, submits that the amount of Tk. 6000/- was paid by the defendants to the plaintiff as security money and the law does not permit and there is no scope for adjusting the said amount towards the realisation or adjustment of rent and hence the courts have committed no error of law in arriving at the finding that the defendants are defaulters and hence liable to be evicted. It is further submitted by Mr. MA Rahim, the learned Advocate for the petitioners, that rents for several months was paid in view of the practice that the defendants used to pay rent and the plaintiff used to accept the rents for several months at a time in lump which is evident from the series of rent receipts and in that view of the matter courts below committed error of law in holding that the defendants were defaulters without considering this aspect of the matter. 

 20. Mr. Rahim in support of his contention has referred to section 10 of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance wherein it has been provided: 

 (a) claim, receive or invite offers or ask for the payment of any premium, salami, fine or any other like sum in addition to the rent, or 

 (b) except with the previous written consent of the Controller, claim or receive the payment of any sum exceeding one month's rent of such premises as rent in advance." 

 The learned Advocate also placed reliance on the case of Shamsuddin Ahmed Vs. Mohd. Hasan and others reported in 31 DLR (AD) 155. In the cited case it is found that a sum of Tk. 19,200/- was given to the landlord as advance rent for 24 months in violation of the provisions of section 10(b). It was submitted in the said case that until the entire amount of Tk. 19,200/- taken by the landlord at the time of creating the tenancy was adjusted, the appellant could not be said to have defaulted in paying rent within the meaning of the provisions of Premises Rent Control Ordinance. It was held that the provisions of section 18(5) of the Ordinance have not been contravened by the appellant rendering him a defaulter in the payment of rent for the premises. 

 21. The case referred to does not help the petitioners in the instant case in any way as the fact and circumstances of the two cases are different and distinguishable. In the instant case the amount said to have been paid by the defendants and received by the plaintiff is not an advance rent but a security deposit and this amount of money does not relate to the terms of any agreement in any way like the case under reference wherein the money was paid as advance rent, and too, forms part of the agreement itself. Taking of money by way of security by the landlord has neither been allowed nor it is prohibited in the Premises Rent Control Ordinance. Now, it is to be seen whether this amount was security money taken by the plaintiff from the defendants or rent paid in advance by the defendants to the plaintiff. From the beginning to the end the plaintiffs clear case was the money received by the plaintiff was a security and it was described as such in the receipt Ext. B. From evidence it will appear that this security was not for the purpose of assuring the payment of rent but as security for keeping the premises in good order. On the other hand, the defendants in their written statement mentioned the amount as loan taken by the plaintiff from the defendants at the time of making construction of structures in the suit premises. During evidence the defendants made a departure from the pleadings and asserted that the money was given as rent by way of advance. The receipt in question (Ext. B) submitted on behalf of the defendants shows the receipt of Tk. 6000/- by the plaintiff with specific mention that it is the security for the room. 

 22. Thus the evidence of the PWs who have categorically mentioned the amount as security deposit finds support from the recital of the receipts itself marked as Ext. B. On the other hand, there is contradictions between the pleading of the defendants at the initial stage and the subsequent version as given out in the deposition by the defendant's witness. Thus I find no hesitation to concur with the findings of the courts below in holding that the receipt speaks nothing more than the admission of the receipt of Tk. 6,000/- as security deposit and not the evidence of payment of rent in advance, and hence the question of getting rent adjusted from the said deposit to avoid default cannot be accepted. The last point argued by the learned Advocate for the petitioner is that the defendants used to pay rent for several months at a time in lump and the plaintiff used to receive the same and such acceptance of rent by the plaintiff will give protection to the defendants from becoming a defaulter for non-payment of rent for a month or two, even if it is so found, but in spite of the said mode of payment of rent the courts below erroneously found that the defendants are defaulter. The record shows that a number of rent receipts and money order receipts showing the remittance have been filed. From perusal of those receipt it is found that the defendants after becoming a defaulter paid rent either directly or remitted by money order and thus there has been violation of sections 18 sub-sec. 5 and 19 of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance in making the payment of rent. Once the defendants became a defaulter subsequent deposit of rent with the House Rent Controller cannot cure this defect so as to give protection to the defaulter from becoming a defaulter. According to the provision of section 18(5) of the Ordinance the tenant must pay the rent within the time fixed in the contract with his landlord or, in the absence or such contract, by the fifteenth day of the month next following that for which the rent becomes due. If the landlord refuses to accept any rent offered within the period mentioned and if the money order so remitted is returned to the tenant by the postal authorities as undelivered being refused by the landlord under the provisions of section 19(a) of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance the tenant is entitled to deposit rent with the House Rent Controller by starting a case within 14 days for the return of the rent to the gender tenant. 

 "The tenant (a monthly tenant) must pay rent in terms of the contract with the landlord of the premises and in the absence of the contract within fifteenth day of the next following month on which the rent falls due, and if the landlord refuses to accept the rent tendered by the tenant, the latter must remit the rent within the aforesaid fifteenth day of the following month by money-order. If the rent remitted by money-order is refused, the tenant can deposit the rent with the Rent Controller within a for night from the date of the receipt of the undelivered rent sent through postal authority, and when these conditions as prescribed in the Ordinance, are fulfilled by the tenant, he gets the protection against ejectment otherwise the protection from ejectment on ground of default in payment of rent granted by the ordinance is clearly taken away by the express language of sub-section (5) of section 18." 

 "Payment of rent in lump (for several months) does not help the tenant from the mischief of default. A tenant by making payment of rent in lump of rent in terms of section 18(1) and 18(5) of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance, 1963 is not protected unless there is a contract to the contrary or such payment is covered by waiver and acquiescence on the part of the landlord." 

 In the instant case it was found by both the courts below that the plea of habitual payment of rent in lump could not give the tenant any protection and does not save him from the mischief of the Rent Control Ordinance making him a defaulter. Furthermore remittance of rent after becoming defaulter and deposit of rent before the House Rent Controller beyond the prescribed period are not in compliance of section 18 and section 19 of the Ordinance and comes within the rule of default as set out in the case referred to above. 

 24. Having regard to the facts and circumstances of the case and evidence on record it is found that the learned Trial Court on consideration of the evidence and materials on record have decreed the suit and the said decree was upheld by the Appellate Court below on consideration of facts and on law as well and I find that the courts below committed no error of law and, therefore, the concurrent finding of facts of two courts below do not call for any interference by this court at this revisional stage.
